title: Exact worst-case convergence of alternating projections with a common interior ball
shortTitle: The worst case is a wedge: exact convergence of alternating projections with a common ball
oneLine: A proof of the Luner–Grimmer conjecture: when two convex sets share a ball, the slowest possible run of alternating projections is exactly a thin two-half-plane wedge, in every dimension, with exact extensions to unequal balls and residuals.
abstract: Alternating projections (von Neumann's method; POCS in signal processing) look for a point in two convex sets by jumping to the nearest point of one set, then of the other. Suppose both sets contain a common ball of radius δ and the start lies within R of its centre. Luner and Grimmer (arXiv:2410.14811, versions 1 and 2, 2024) built two half-planes for which the distance to the intersection after N cycles equals max over 0 ≤ c ≤ κ of c^(2N−1)(√(R²−δ²) − δ√((1+c)/(1−c))), with κ = 1 − 2δ²/R², and conjectured that nothing is worse. This candidate proves the conjecture for every N in every dimension with a short hand-checkable argument: each trajectory is tracked by two numbers, compared with the half-plane trajectory through a monotone value function, and closed with a sharp error bound. The same argument gives the exact worst case for balls of different radii about a common centre, after any number (at least two) of single projections and in real Hilbert space (Theorem 7), and the exact worst residual, which recovers the exact rate of Zamani and Glineur (2024) as δ → 0 (Theorem 8). Consequences include the sharp equivalent R⁴κ^(2N)/(8eδ²√(R²−δ²)N), a limiting profile, a computable stopping test and practical cycle counts: at R/δ = 10 and accuracy 10⁻³ the exact worst case needs 93 cycles, against 212 from an elementary bound with the sharp factor and 833 from the classical interior-point bound. The formula and the extremal half-planes are Luner and Grimmer's; the contribution is the matching upper bound and the extensions. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Exact worst case (Theorem 1, proof): for closed convex sets in any dimension containing a common ball of radius δ, with the start within R of its centre, the distance to the intersection after N ≥ 1 cycles is at most max over 0 ≤ c ≤ κ of c^(2N−1)(√(R²−δ²) − δ√((1+c)/(1−c))), κ = 1 − 2δ²/R², and two half-planes attain it; if R ≤ √2·δ one cycle suffices. This proves Conjecture 6.2 of Luner and Grimmer (2024), whose formula and construction these are.

Extensions (Theorems 7 and 8, proof): exact worst cases for balls of different radii a and b about a common centre, after any number k ≥ 2 of single projections, in real Hilbert space; and the exact worst residual, which tends to the Zamani–Glineur (2024) rate as δ → 0.

Sharp asymptotics (Corollaries 5-6, proof): W_N ~ R⁴κ^(2N)/(8eδ²√(R²−δ²)N); a limiting profile when Nδ²/R² is held fixed; after the first projection, near-worst instances lie only Θ(1/N) from the intersection.

In practice (Section 9): at R/δ = 10 and accuracy 10⁻³ the exact worst case needs 93 cycles, against 212 from an elementary bound with the sharp factor κ and 833 from the classical interior-point bound; Lemma 3 also gives a computable stopping test for any run.

narration: How slow can alternating projections be? An Evidence Press briefing. Many practical problems ask for a point that satisfies two constraints at once: for example, an image that matches measured data and also has no negative brightness. A classic way to find one is to jump back and forth. Move to the nearest point that satisfies the first constraint, then to the nearest point that satisfies the second, and repeat. This is von Neumann's method of alternating projections, known in signal processing as POCS. It works when the constraints are convex, but it can be slow. Suppose both constraint sets contain a common ball of some radius, and the starting point is within a known distance of its centre. In 2024, Alan Luner and Benjamin Grimmer found a simple pair of straight-edged sets, a thin wedge, that makes the method very slow, and conjectured that nothing is ever worse. This paper proves their conjecture, in every number of dimensions, with a short argument that can be checked by hand. The worst case is exactly that wedge: the iterates zig-zag towards its corner, getting closer by the same factor at every step. The same argument also gives exact answers for balls of different sizes about the same centre, and for other measures of progress. In practice the difference is large. With a starting distance ten times the ball's radius, getting within one thousandth of that distance of a solution takes at most ninety-three cycles in the worst case, whereas the classical guarantee asks for eight hundred and thirty-three. The formula and the wedge are Luner and Grimmer's; what is new is the proof that nothing is worse. The proofs are written out in full, and nearly ninety thousand computer checks in exact or high-precision arithmetic back them up. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or formally verified. Published on the third of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: How many cycles of alternating projections are enough, in the worst case, when two convex sets share a ball of radius δ and the start lies within R of its centre: the exact count from the Luner–Grimmer formula, now proved to be an upper bound.
decisionObject.scope: Two closed convex sets with a common interior ball (or balls with a common centre), exact unrelaxed projections, any dimension or real Hilbert space. Three or more sets, relaxed projections and different centres are not covered.
